questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. A step with no record, tested once or routinely
questions.question: At a Ghanaian pharmacy chain, a second pharmacist must witness each opening of the controlled-drug safe, and nothing records the witness. Which method BEST lets internal auditor Efua test whether witnessing routinely happens?

options.A: Walk through one safe opening with the pharmacist on duty
options.B: Interview the pharmacists who open the safe on each shift
options.C: Observe openings at unannounced times over several shifts
options.D: Inspect the written safe procedure and its approval record

questions.key_concept: When a step leaves no record, observation is the source, and showing it is routine takes repeated observation, not one walk-through.
questions.pre_read: Does the question ask whether the step can be done, or whether it is done routinely? Which source could show each?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information that is relevant and sufficient, and its considerations list directly observing a process as one way to gather it. The witnessing step leaves no record, so observation is the source, and seeing several openings at unannounced times shows whether it happens routinely rather than only when staff expect a visit. One walk-through, the closest choice, shows the step done once, with notice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a walk-through observes the step, but one opening with notice shows only that it can be done. It cannot show that witnessing happens routinely.
wrong_explanations.B: Interviews show what pharmacists say they do. Statements from the people performing the step need corroboration and cannot show by themselves that witnessing happens.
wrong_explanations.D: The written procedure is the criteria: it shows what should happen. It cannot show whether pharmacists actually witness openings in practice.

tips: Eliminate: B, because pharmacists' own statements need corroboration before they show practice, and D, because the procedure states the criteria, not what happens.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.1 asks for sufficient information; one announced walk-through shows the step once, while observation on several shifts shows whether it is routine.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a single walk-through shows how a step works. Whether it happens routinely needs repeated observation or records across the period.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B1.3 Fitting the Source to the Objective. Sources opened 25 Nov 2026: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.1 (requirements: information is relevant and sufficient; considerations: procedures include directly observing a process, also known as a walk-through) and the CIA Part 2 syllabus, bullet 2B1a (interviews, observations, walk-throughs and data analyses). Unannounced timing is sound practice that supports the key; the key rests on sufficiency. Original scenario; no IIA practice question or prep-bank text used. Part 2 pilot, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Sources of engagement information. An objective about what staff know
questions.question: An engagement at a Chilean mining firm's 60 sites asks whether site staff know how to raise a safety incident under the new policy. Which source BEST serves internal auditor Ignacio?

options.A: A questionnaire asking sampled staff how they would raise one
options.B: The incident log, showing how many reports each site filed
options.C: Site managers' signed checklists confirming staff were briefed
options.D: The approved policy and the training plan that rolled it out

questions.key_concept: Relevance comes from the objective: when the question is what staff know, asking staff to show that knowledge is direct evidence of the condition.
questions.pre_read: What exactly does the objective ask about: what was done, what was planned, or what people know?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 makes information relevant when it fits the engagement objective, and its considerations list surveying the people involved as a way to gather it. Here the condition is what staff know, so asking a sample of staff how they would raise an incident tests that knowledge directly. Managers' signed checklists, the closest choice, show that briefings were held, not that the people briefed know the route.

wrong_explanations.B: A count of reports filed shows activity, not knowledge. A site with few reports may simply have had few incidents, so the log cannot show what staff know.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the checklists show that briefings happened, as the managers report them. Being briefed is not the same as knowing, and the objective asks about knowledge.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy and training plan describe what should happen. They are the criteria, not evidence of what staff at the 60 sites actually know.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a count of reports shows how often incidents were filed, not whether staff know how, and D, because the policy and plan state the criteria.
Final two: A beats C because the objective is staff knowledge; a questionnaire tests it directly, while a checklist records only that a briefing took place.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, let the objective pick the source. When the condition is what people know or believe, asking them is direct evidence, not a weak substitute.
questions.framework_ref: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.1 Gathering Information for Analyses and Evaluation; CIA Part 2 syllabus (2025), Expanded Test Specifications V2.09.2024 FINAL
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B1.2 Documents as Sources of Information. Sources opened 25 Nov 2026: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.1 (requirements: relevant information is consistent with the engagement objectives; considerations: procedures include interviewing or surveying individuals involved in the activity) and the CIA Part 2 syllabus, bullet 2B1b (policies, checklists, risk and control questionnaires and self-assessment surveys). Bullet 2B1b. New lesson: when the objective is what people know, a questionnaire is the relevant source, and a checklist of briefings or the policy is not. Nearest Part 1 items: cia1_d3_003 (evidence of culture must be relevant to the objective; different objective and trap) and cia1_d1_097 (a self-assessment relied on once checked). questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A whole population from an editable file
questions.question: A Kenyan county's procurement head emails internal auditor Wanjiru a spreadsheet of all 4,200 purchase orders, kept and editable by the head's team; matching every row shows each order approved. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Enough to conclude: every order was tested, not a sample
options.B: Enough to conclude once totals match the team's monthly reports
options.C: Not enough yet: suppliers should confirm each order's delivery
options.D: Not enough yet: the audited team holds and can alter the file

questions.key_concept: A full-population test is only as good as its data: rows the audited team can change are checked against the source before relying on them.
questions.pre_read: Before counting how much was tested, ask who produced the data and whether it could have been changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 says reliability is strengthened when the internal auditor obtains information directly, or from a system with effective controls, and Standard 4.3 requires critically assessing reliability. Rows the audited team keeps and can change are neither, so testing all 4,200 adds coverage, not trust. Whole-population testing, the closest choice, is only as good as its data: Wanjiru should take the orders from the purchasing system directly before concluding.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: testing every row removes sampling risk, but not the risk that the rows were altered. Volume never makes up for information that is not yet reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Both documents come from the same team, so agreement between them is not independent corroboration. A file and reports from one source can match and both be wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Delivery confirmations bear on whether goods arrived, not on whether orders were approved. They come from an outside party, but they do not fit this objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because two records from the same team do not corroborate each other independently, and C, because delivery evidence does not answer whether orders were approved.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.1 ties reliability to who obtained the data and the system behind it; testing every row of an editable file tests the file, not the orders.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a full-population test inherits the quality of its data. Ask who produced the file and whether it could be changed before trusting the count.

Sources opened 25 Nov 2026: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.1 (requirements: information is relevant, reliable and sufficient; reliability is strengthened when obtained directly by an internal auditor, corroborated, or gathered from a system with effective controls) and Standard 4.3 (requirements: critically assess the reliability of information). questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A first-hand extract from a weakly controlled system
questions.question: Internal auditor Rangi queried a New Zealand hospital's pharmacy stock system directly; a review last month found staff can overwrite quantities with no log or review. Which view of the results is MOST accurate?

options.A: Strong: Rangi obtained the quantities first-hand from the system
options.B: Weakened: the system behind them lacks effective controls
options.C: Weakened: the pharmacy, not internal audit, owns the system
options.D: Strong: the figures are current and come from the official record

questions.key_concept: Reliability has three separate factors; getting data first-hand does not repair figures held in a system whose controls over changes are missing.
questions.pre_read: Check each reliability factor on its own: who obtained the data, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 names three things that strengthen reliability: the internal auditor obtaining information directly or from an independent source, corroboration, and a system with effective governance, risk management and control processes. Rangi's first-hand query meets the first, but quantities anyone can overwrite unseen fail the third, so the figures need corroboration, such as a count, before use. First-hand retrieval, the closest choice, cannot repair weak data at its source.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: obtaining data directly does strengthen reliability, but only for how it was retrieved. Quantities that staff can change unseen may be wrong before Rangi's query runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Activities usually own the systems internal audit queries. Ownership does not weaken a first-hand extract; the missing controls over changes do.
wrong_explanations.D: Current, official figures are reliable only when the system that holds them is well controlled. Here last month's review found the controls over changes missing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the activity owning a system is normal and does not weaken a first-hand query, and D, because official figures are only as good as the controls over them.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.1 counts the system behind the data as its own reliability factor; retrieving it first-hand does not fix figures anyone can overwrite.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, test all three reliability factors separately: who obtained it, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Judging the quality of evidence. A sample the activity selected
questions.question: Internal auditor Kasia tested 25 of a Polish retailer's 610 vendor master changes, the size the methodology sets; the vendor team lead selected them, and all were authorized. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Too weak for the 610: the activity, not Kasia, picked the items
options.B: Too weak for the 610: 25 items cannot represent so many changes
options.C: Enough for the 610: each tested change carried the required approval
options.D: Enough for the 610: another auditor could repeat Kasia's 25 tests

questions.key_concept: Sufficient means a competent reviewer would reach the same conclusion about the whole population, which a sample chosen by the activity may not represent.
questions.pre_read: Ask what population the conclusion covers, and whether the items tested were chosen so that they stand for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.1, evidence is sufficient when someone careful, informed and capable could redo the work program and arrive at the same conclusions, and its considerations say a sample should be as representative of the population as possible. Items the activity picked may leave out the changes that matter. Repeating the 25 tests, the closest choice, would only confirm those 25; it says nothing yet about the other 585.

wrong_explanations.B: The methodology sets 25 for this population, so size is not the gap. A sample of that size can support a conclusion when it is chosen to represent all changes.
wrong_explanations.C: The tests show those 25 were authorized. A clean result speaks for all 610 only if the sample represents them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: repeatability is part of the test, but the reviewer must also reach the same conclusion about all 610. Redoing a hand-picked sample does not get there.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the methodology already sets 25 for this population, and C, because a clean result on 25 items speaks for all 610 only if they represent the rest.
Final two: A beats D because Standard 14.1's reviewer must reach the same conclusion, not just the same 25 results; a sample the activity chose may not represent the year.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about sufficiency, ask who chose the items and what population they stand for. A sample supports only what it represents.

Sources opened 25 Nov 2026: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.1 (requirements: sufficient information enables a prudent, informed and competent person to repeat the work program and reach the same conclusions; considerations: a sample should be as representative of the entire population as possible), Standard 13.6 (considerations: the work program records the sampling method, population and sample size) and Standard 14.6. questions.subtopic: 2B3 Technology tools for audit work. A clean dashboard from management's monitoring
questions.question: A Brazilian airline's revenue team runs continuous monitoring over ticket refunds, and its dashboard has shown no exceptions all year. How should internal auditor Thiago BEST treat the dashboard in a refunds engagement?

options.A: Rely on it, since the revenue team reviews it every week
options.B: Ask the revenue team to widen its rules before the work starts
options.C: Test its rules and data before relying on its clean result
options.D: Take over running the monitoring for the rest of the year

questions.key_concept: A clean result from management's monitoring is information to assess: test its rules and data before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Who runs the dashboard, and what would it show if its rules missed a kind of improper refund?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 requires internal auditors to critically assess the reliability of information, and Standard 14.1 ties reliability to how information was obtained and the controls behind it. A clean dashboard is management's monitoring output, only as good as its rules and the data fed to it, so Thiago tests both before relying on it. Weekly review by the team, the closest choice, shows the dashboard is read, not that its rules catch improper refunds.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: management's weekly review shows the dashboard is watched, not that it works. Rules that miss a kind of improper refund report nothing, however often someone looks.
wrong_explanations.B: How management sets up its own monitoring is management's decision. Internal audit first judges whether the output can be relied on; any recommendation follows the evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Monitoring that works as a control belongs to management. Running it would put internal audit in charge of a control it is meant to assess.

tips: Eliminate: B, because management sets its own monitoring rules and recommendations follow evidence, and D, because running management's monitoring would make internal audit operate a control it assesses.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 4.3 requires assessing reliability before relying; a dashboard someone reviews is still only as good as its rules and data.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, treat a tool's output as information to assess, not a conclusion. Check its rules and data before a clean result counts as evidence.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. A walk-through that contradicts the approved map
questions.question: At a Turkish retailer, management's approved map shows a supervisor approving every credit note; internal auditor Elif's walk-through of three small notes found none approved. What is the BEST basis for the condition?

options.A: The approved map, treating the three notes as exceptions
options.B: The practice observed in the walk-through of real notes
options.C: The process the billing clerks describe when interviewed
options.D: The billing policy on which credit notes need approval

questions.key_concept: The condition is what evidence shows the process does; a map, however approved, shows the design management intends.
questions.pre_read: Which of these shows how the process is meant to run, and which shows how it actually runs?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires the condition to be determined from information and evidence gathered during the engagement. Following real credit notes through the process is first-hand evidence of how it runs, so the observed practice is the condition. The approved map, the closest choice, shows how management says the process should run; calling three unapproved notes exceptions assumes a result the testing has not shown.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an approved map shows the intended design, which can inform the criteria. Three walk-throughs that all contradict it are evidence about the condition, not exceptions to set aside.
wrong_explanations.C: What clerks describe is a statement that needs corroboration. The walk-through has already shown the real practice, so the clerks' account cannot override it.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy says which notes need approval, which makes it criteria. The condition is what actually happens, and that comes from evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because interview statements need corroboration and cannot outweigh what was observed, and D, because a policy sets the criteria, not the condition.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.2 sets the condition from evidence gathered; an approved map is management's design, and three contrary walk-throughs are evidence, not exceptions.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a process map is a claim about design until real items are walked through it. Condition comes from evidence; criteria from what should be.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. Entries flagged by anomaly detection
questions.question: Anomaly detection on a Vietnamese manufacturer's 90,000 journal entries flags 160 as out of pattern, such as weekend postings. Which next step is BEST for internal auditor Linh?

options.A: Log the 160 as potential findings, then ask staff to explain each
options.B: Ask the controller to reverse the 160 entries before closing
options.C: Retune the tool's settings until fewer entries are flagged
options.D: Check each flagged entry against the posting policy and support

questions.key_concept: An analytics flag shows an entry is unusual; it becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows it differs from the criteria.
questions.pre_read: Is an unusual entry the same thing as an entry that breaks a rule?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2, a potential finding is a gap between what the criteria require and the condition the evidence shows. An entry flagged as unusual has broken a pattern, not yet a rule: a weekend posting may be allowed. Checking each against the posting policy and its support shows which ones differ from the criteria. Logging all 160 as potential findings first, the closest choice, treats the tool's pattern as the criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: following up is right, but labeling all 160 as potential findings first treats unusual as wrong. Only a difference from the criteria makes a potential finding.
wrong_explanations.B: Correcting entries is management's decision, and only once an entry is shown to be wrong. Reversing entries no one has examined could undo valid postings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tuning can cut false alarms later, once follow-up shows which flags were valid. Changing settings now would drop entries before anyone has checked them.

tips: Eliminate: B, because correcting entries is management's call once an error is shown, and C, because retuning before follow-up drops entries no one has examined.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.2 makes a potential finding a difference from the criteria; a flag only shows an entry is unusual until it is checked against the rule.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an analytics flag is a lead. It becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows the condition differs from the criteria.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. Supplier names spelled several ways
questions.question: To find duplicate supplier payments at a Singapore firm, internal auditor Wei extracted a year of payments; many suppliers appear under several spellings, such as 'Tan Ltd' and 'TAN LIMITED'. What should Wei do FIRST?

options.A: Standardize the supplier names and agree totals to the ledger
options.B: Run the duplicate test now and sort out spellings in follow-up
options.C: Delete repeated rows so the totals no longer double count
options.D: Show the payables managers the raw extract and ask for comments

questions.key_concept: Normalizing comes before analyzing: data is made consistent and agreed to its source before any test runs on it.
questions.pre_read: Where does this task sit in the analytics steps: objective, data, normalize, analyze, communicate?
questions.correct_explanation: The Part 2 syllabus orders the analytics steps as setting the objective, obtaining relevant data, normalizing it, analyzing it and communicating results, and Standard 14.2 requires analyses to use reliable information. With one supplier under several spellings, a match would miss duplicates paid under different names, so Wei first standardizes the names and agrees the extract's total to its source. Testing now, the closest choice, builds the analysis on data that cannot yet be compared.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: speed is tempting, but a match across inconsistent names misses duplicates paid under another spelling. Follow-up cannot repair an analysis built on data never made consistent.
wrong_explanations.C: Repeated rows may be the duplicate payments the test exists to find. Normalizing makes records consistent; it does not remove the ones that look awkward.
wrong_explanations.D: Results go to management after analysis and follow-up. A raw extract shows nothing yet and spends the managers' time before there is anything to discuss.

tips: Eliminate: C, because repeated rows may be the very duplicates being sought, and D, because results are shared after analysis, not as a raw extract.
Final two: A beats B because normalizing comes before analyzing: Standard 14.2 needs reliable information, and names in several spellings cannot be matched reliably.
Exam cue: on CIA analytics questions, follow the order: objective, data, normalize, analyze, communicate. When records do not line up, make them consistent before testing.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Analytics and process mapping. An answer held in unstructured contract text
questions.question: At a South African miner, internal auditor Thandi must learn whether supplier contracts hold the required anti-bribery clause; the contract system stores dates, values and parties, plus each contract's text. Which analysis BEST fits?

options.A: Query the system's structured fields, which cover every contract
options.B: Read 30 contracts from the largest unit, clause by clause
options.C: Search the text of every contract for the clause's wording
options.D: Compare contract values with those of other mining groups

questions.key_concept: Find where the answer is recorded before choosing the method: when it sits in free text, text analysis of the unstructured data fits.
questions.pre_read: Which data source could actually show whether a contract contains the clause?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information consistent with the engagement objective. The question is what each contract says, and the structured fields hold only dates, values and parties, so the answer sits in the contract text: unstructured data that text analysis can search for the clause's wording across every contract. Querying the structured fields, the closest choice, uses complete, tidy data that cannot show whether the clause is there.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the structured fields cover every contract, but none records the clause. Complete data that does not hold the answer is not relevant to this objective.
wrong_explanations.B: Reading contracts is the right source, but 30 from one unit cannot speak for every contract. A text search covers the whole population at little cost.
wrong_explanations.D: Other groups' contract values say nothing about whether this group's contracts contain the clause. The comparison does not bear on the objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because 30 contracts from one unit do not represent all contracts, and D, because other groups' contract values do not show what these contracts say.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.1 asks for information that fits the objective; the fields cover every contract but hold nothing about the clause, which sits in the text.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, find where the answer is recorded before picking the method. Free text is unstructured data, and text analysis is how to read it at scale.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. An expectation built from pay and headcount
questions.question: A Mexican retailer's payroll cost rose 12%; the only pay change was a 4% award, and average headcount fell 3%. Which expectation should internal auditor Paola BEST test the rise against?

options.A: About 4%, since the pay award applies to every employee
options.B: About 7%, adding the award and the fall in headcount
options.C: About 3% lower, since fewer employees are on the payroll
options.D: About 1%, the award offset by the fall in headcount

questions.key_concept: Analytical review compares actual figures with an expectation built from every known driver, so the gap left to explain is the real one.
questions.pre_read: Which known facts push payroll cost up, and which push it down?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations include analyzing financial information, such as payroll expense, against nonfinancial information, such as the average number of employees. A 4% award paid to about 3% fewer people points to a rise of about 1%, so most of the 12% rise is unexplained and needs follow-up before any view is formed. The award alone, the closest choice, leaves out the drop in headcount that should have pulled cost down.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the award is one driver, but fewer employees should lower total pay. Ignoring headcount sets the expectation too high and hides part of the gap.
wrong_explanations.B: Headcount fell, so it pulls cost down, not up. Adding the two drivers compounds the error instead of offsetting it.
wrong_explanations.C: Fewer employees is one driver, but each remaining employee earns about 4% more. Ignoring the award sets the expectation too low.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a fall in headcount lowers cost rather than adding to it, and C, because each remaining employee still received the 4% award.
Final two: D beats A because a sound expectation uses every known driver; the award raises cost and the smaller headcount lowers it, leaving about 1%.
Exam cue: on CIA analytical review questions, build the expectation from the known nonfinancial drivers first, then measure the gap the follow-up must explain.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Analytical review techniques. A technique for comparing similar units
questions.question: A Canadian city asks whether its four similar-sized parking garages are run at comparable cost for each vehicle served; barrier counters log each departure. Which technique BEST serves internal auditor Owen?

options.A: Each garage's costs this year against its own prior year
options.B: Each garage's cost per vehicle against the other garages
options.C: Each garage's costs against the budget the city set for it
options.D: Each garage's barrier counts matched to its paid exits

questions.key_concept: The objective picks the analytic: for relative efficiency, compare a unit cost across similar units; trends, budgets and completeness tests answer other questions.
questions.pre_read: Is the question about change over time, results against plan, complete revenue, or how similar units compare?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations list internal benchmarking, comparing information between areas of the same organization, among the analyses a work program may use. The question is relative efficiency, so cost per vehicle across four similar garages answers it directly, and their similar size keeps the comparison fair. A trend against each garage's prior year, the closest choice, shows whether costs changed, not whether one garage costs more than the others.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a trend shows how each garage's costs moved, but all four could rise together and still differ widely. It does not compare the garages with one another.
wrong_explanations.C: A budget variance measures results against the plan. Each garage could meet a budget set on its own past costs while costing far more per vehicle than the others.
wrong_explanations.D: Matching barrier counts to paid exits tests whether every vehicle paid, which suits a question about complete revenue. It says nothing about the cost of running each garage.

tips: Eliminate: C, because meeting a budget does not show how the garages compare on cost, and D, because matching counts to paid exits tests complete revenue, not cost.
Final two: B beats A because the objective asks how the garages compare with one another; a trend compares each garage only with its own past.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, let the objective pick the analytic: similar units side by side for efficiency, trends for change over time, independent counts for completeness.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. More testing for a thinly supported gap
questions.question: Internal auditor Sipho's approved program tests 25 of a Botswana utility's 900 meter replacements; three lacked the required sign-off, and Sipho wants to test 75 more. Which action BEST meets the Standards?

options.A: Test the 75 now and note the extension for the supervisor's review
options.B: Report the three as a finding now, noting the sample was small
options.C: Adjust the program and get it approved before testing the 75
options.D: Set the three aside until the next engagement on meter work

questions.key_concept: When more analysis is needed to support a potential finding, the work program is adjusted and approved before the added work, not reviewed after it.
questions.pre_read: Who approves a change to the work program, and does the approval come before or after the work?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires due professional care in deciding whether more analysis is needed, and when it is, the program is changed and the change approved by the chief audit executive. So Sipho gets the change approved, by the chief audit executive or a supervisor the chief audit executive delegates to, before testing the extra 75. Testing first and noting it for review, the closest choice, turns a required approval into an after-the-fact check.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the extra testing is sound, but Standard 14.2 has the adjusted program approved before the work. A later review is not the approval the Standard requires.
wrong_explanations.B: Three exceptions show a difference, but Sipho wants more evidence of its extent. Reporting now would rest the finding on evidence Sipho already finds too thin.
wrong_explanations.D: A difference between criteria and condition must be noted and evaluated in this engagement. Deferring it to a later one leaves a known potential finding unresolved.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Sipho already judges the evidence too thin to show the gap's extent, and D, because a potential finding is evaluated in this engagement, not deferred.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.2 requires the adjusted program to be approved before the added analysis; review afterward is not approval.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, added testing means a changed work program, and a changed program is approved before the work by the chief audit executive or a delegate.

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Stating the effect when no loss has occurred
questions.question: At a Philippine lender, internal auditor Marisol finds 14 loan officers can change borrowers' bank details without review; tests found no misuse this year. Which BEST states the finding's effect?

options.A: Loan payouts could be redirected to accounts no one has checked
options.B: None so far, since tests found no misuse during the year
options.C: The breach of the policy requiring review of detail changes
options.D: The cost of the review step management would need to add

questions.key_concept: A finding's effect is the potential exposure the gap creates; it exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has happened.
questions.pre_read: Keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria, condition, root cause and effect. Which one is each option describing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires internal auditors to determine the potential effects of each potential finding, and its considerations describe the effect as the risk or potential exposure, often estimated with input from management. Payouts that could go to accounts no one checks are that exposure, whether or not misuse has happened yet. No effect, the closest choice, confuses what has happened with what could happen.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: no misuse found is good news, but the effect is the potential exposure. A gap that could let payouts be redirected matters before any loss occurs.
wrong_explanations.C: Unreviewed changes measured against the policy are the condition and the criteria of the finding. The effect is what that gap could cause.
wrong_explanations.D: The cost of a fix matters when weighing recommendations or action plans. It is not the effect of the gap.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the gap between policy and practice is the condition against the criteria, and D, because the cost of a fix belongs to weighing the action, not the effect.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 14.3 asks for potential effects; an exposure exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has occurred yet.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria (what should be), condition (what is), root cause (why) and effect (what could result).

questions.subtopic: 2B6 Findings and their significance. Ranking findings with the function's methodology
questions.question: Internal auditor Javier finds the function's rating scale too coarse for a Spanish port's engagement, and the port's manager asks that findings be ranked by cost to fix. How should Javier BEST rank them?

options.A: By the cost to fix, as the port's manager requests
options.B: By the money at stake, the measure the board reads most easily
options.C: On a finer scale fitted to this engagement, explained in the report
options.D: On the function's scale, raising its coarseness separately

questions.key_concept: Findings are ranked with the chief audit executive's methodology so ratings stay consistent across engagements; a better method is proposed, not used alone.
questions.pre_read: Who sets the method for rating findings, and what would a different scale do to comparisons with other engagements?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires each finding to be ranked by significance with the chief audit executive's methodology, and its considerations say this keeps ratings consistent across engagements. Javier rates on the function's scale and takes the view that it is too coarse to the chief audit executive, who owns the method. A scale fitted to this engagement, the closest choice, sounds careful but makes these ratings mean something different from every other engagement's.

wrong_explanations.A: Cost to fix can help management order its action plans. Significance rests on likelihood and impact, so the manager's preference does not set the ranking.
wrong_explanations.B: Money is one part of impact. Significance also weighs likelihood and other factors, so ranking by money alone can misrank a small but serious gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a finer scale may describe this engagement better, but Standard 14.3 requires the chief audit executive's methodology. A private scale breaks consistency across engagements.

tips: Eliminate: A, because significance rests on likelihood and impact rather than the cost of a fix, and B, because money alone leaves out likelihood and the nature of the risk.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 14.3 requires prioritizing with the chief audit executive's methodology; a better scale is proposed to the chief audit executive, not used alone.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor applies the function's methodology and proposes changes to it; changing it alone for one engagement is the trap.
questions.framework_ref: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 14.3 Evaluation of Findings; Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 9.3 Methodologies

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A workpaper that keeps only the exceptions
questions.question: To keep a file short, internal auditor Tomas saved only the 4 exceptions from 60 claim payments tested at an Israeli insurer. What does the workpaper MOST need?

options.A: Tomas's initials and the date each test was carried out
options.B: The population, selection, checks and result for all 60 items
options.C: The claims manager's written agreement with each of the 4 exceptions
options.D: The engagement risk assessment that led to this test

questions.key_concept: A complete workpaper lets another competent auditor repeat the test: the population, how items were chosen, what was checked and every result.
questions.pre_read: Could another auditor redo this test from the file alone, and if not, what is missing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires the work to be documented well enough that another informed, careful internal auditor could redo it and get the same results. With only the exceptions kept, no one can see the population, how the 60 were chosen, what was checked or what the other 56 showed. Initials and dates, the closest choice, should be recorded too, but they show who did the work, not what was done.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: initials of who performed the work belong in the file, but they do not let a reviewer repeat a test whose population and passing items are missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Discussing exceptions with management is part of the work, but agreement on 4 items does not show what the other 56 were or how they were chosen.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk assessment belongs in the engagement file, but it does not record what this test covered, how items were chosen or what each showed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because management's agreement covers the 4 exceptions but not the 56 that passed, and D, because the risk assessment explains why the test exists, not what it found.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.6 requires enough to repeat the work; initials show who tested, while the population, selection and results show what was tested.
Exam cue: on CIA workpaper questions, apply the stranger test: could another competent auditor redo the work from the file alone and get the same result?

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A reported figure with no support on file
questions.question: Internal auditor Chiamaka's draft finding at a Nigerian telecom states roaming losses of $2.1 million, a figure the finance director gave in a call; nothing in the workpapers supports it. Which action is BEST?

options.A: Keep the figure as stated, attributing it to the finance director
options.B: Keep the figure, since a senior manager stated it directly
options.C: Support the figure with evidence on file before the draft goes out
options.D: Remove the whole finding, since its figure lacks support

questions.key_concept: Every figure in a result must trace to documented evidence; a statement heard in a call is corroborated and filed before it supports a draft.
questions.pre_read: Can a reader trace this number from the draft back to a workpaper, and is a statement in a call evidence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires internal auditors to document the information and evidence that support engagement results, and Standard 4.3 requires seeking more evidence for statements that might be incomplete or wrong. A loss figure heard in a call is a statement, so Chiamaka obtains support, such as the roaming ledger, and files it before the draft goes out. Attributing the figure, the closest choice, reports an unchecked number with a label on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: attribution tells readers where the number came from, but the result still rests on an unverified figure. Standard 14.6 needs the supporting evidence on file.
wrong_explanations.B: Seniority does not make a statement evidence. A figure from a call needs corroboration and documentation before it supports a result.
wrong_explanations.D: The gap is the figure's support, not necessarily the finding. If the rest of the finding is supported, removing all of it would drop a result the evidence backs.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a senior manager's statement still needs corroboration, and D, because an unsupported figure calls for support, not for dropping a finding the evidence may back.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.6 requires results to rest on documented evidence; naming who said a figure does not make it supported.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, trace every number and claim in a draft back to a workpaper. If the trail breaks, support it or narrow it before the draft goes out.

questions.subtopic: 2B7 Workpapers that support the results. A retention period set by law and by policy
questions.question: Closing an engagement file at a Dutch pension fund, internal auditor Sanne sees that the law requires keeping such records at least five years and the function's policy says seven. Which retention is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Seven years, which meets both the law and the policy
options.B: Five years, as the law takes priority over internal policy
options.C: Five years, then disposal to reduce the records held
options.D: Seven years, once legal counsel has confirmed the choice

questions.key_concept: Engagement records are kept to law and regulation and to the function's and organization's policies together; a legal minimum does not cap a longer policy.
questions.pre_read: Do the law and the policy actually conflict here, or can both be met at once?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires engagement records to be kept as the relevant laws and regulations require, and as the function's and the organization's own policies require. A legal minimum of five years and a policy of seven do not conflict: keeping the file seven years meets both. Five years, the closest choice, treats the law's minimum as a cap and breaks the function's own policy.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the law sets a minimum, not a limit, so there is no conflict to resolve. Disposing at five years would break the function's seven-year policy.
wrong_explanations.C: Disposal to reduce records held is right when no rule requires keeping them. Here the policy requires seven years, and early disposal would leave the results without support.
wrong_explanations.D: Counsel's advice helps the chief audit executive where legal rules are unclear or pull against policy. Here both rules are clear and are met together by keeping seven years.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the policy still requires the file after five years, and D, because both rules are clear and can be met together, so there is nothing for counsel to settle.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 14.6 binds retention to laws and to the function's policies together; a legal minimum of five years does not cap a seven-year policy.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check whether rules truly conflict before choosing one. When every rule can be met at once, the requirement is to meet them all.

questions.subtopic: 2B8 Reaching engagement conclusions. Minor gaps that together weaken one control aim
questions.question: Internal auditor Bilal's engagement on a Jordanian airport's fuel stock found three low-rated gaps: late stock counts, unreconciled meter readings and unreviewed loss reports. Which overall conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Satisfactory, since each finding on its own is rated low
options.B: Not satisfactory, since the three gaps all weaken how losses are caught
options.C: Satisfactory, with the three gaps reported as one combined finding
options.D: No overall view, since the gaps sit in three separate controls

questions.key_concept: The conclusion weighs findings together: several minor gaps that affect the same aim can add up to a conclusion that is not satisfactory.
questions.pre_read: Look past each finding's own rating: what do the three gaps have in common, and what does that mean taken together?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.5 requires the conclusion to state the internal auditor's view of how significant the findings are when taken together. Late counts, unreconciled meter readings and unreviewed loss reports are each minor, but they are the ways fuel losses are caught, so together they let losses go unnoticed. Reporting one combined finding while still concluding satisfactory, the closest choice, weighs them together in a finding but not in the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating each finding alone is the first step, not the conclusion. Standard 14.5 asks for the overall significance of the findings taken together.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: combining the gaps shows the right instinct, but concluding satisfactory ignores what the combination means for catching losses. The conclusion must carry the aggregate judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: An engagement conclusion is required, and it covers the findings as a whole. Findings in separate controls can still bear on the same risk.

tips: Eliminate: A, because rating findings one by one is not weighing them together, and D, because Standard 14.5 requires an overall conclusion whatever controls the findings sit in.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 14.5 puts the aggregate judgment in the conclusion itself; naming a combined finding while concluding satisfactory leaves the conclusion unweighed.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, weigh findings together, not one by one: several minor gaps on the same risk can add up to a conclusion that is not satisfactory.

questions.subtopic: 2B8 Reaching engagement conclusions. A conclusion that only lists findings
questions.question: Internal auditor Mei's draft conclusion for an assurance engagement on a Taiwanese chipmaker's payroll lists three rated findings with root causes and stops; there were no scope limitations. What does it MOST lack?

options.A: Management's action plans, with owners and due dates
options.B: An explanation of any limits placed on the scope
options.C: The criteria and condition behind each of the findings
options.D: A judgment on how effective the payroll controls are overall

questions.key_concept: An assurance conclusion is the auditor's overall judgment on how effective governance, risk management and controls are; a list of findings is not a conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Which of these belongs in the conclusion itself, and which belongs elsewhere in the final communication?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.5, an assurance conclusion sums up the results against the engagement's objectives and management's, and says how effective the activity's governance, risk management and control processes are. A list of rated findings leaves that judgment unstated. Action plans with owners and dates, the closest choice, are required in the final communication under Standard 15.1, but they are not part of the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 15.1 requires owners and dates in the final communication, but they record management's response. The conclusion is the internal auditor's own overall judgment.
wrong_explanations.B: Scope limitations are explained when there are any. Mei's engagement had none, so nothing is missing here.
wrong_explanations.C: Criteria and condition belong in each finding, and Mei's findings already carry root causes. The gap is the overall judgment, not more detail on single findings.

tips: Eliminate: B, because there were no scope limitations to explain, and C, because more detail on each finding still leaves the overall judgment unstated.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.5 makes the effectiveness judgment part of an assurance conclusion; owners and dates are final communication content under Standard 15.1.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a list of findings is not a conclusion. An assurance conclusion says how well the processes work, including when they work.
